summary: A chanson of treachery, pride, and vengeance: Roland's honor refuses the horn, the peers die at Roncevaux, and Charlemagne weeps while justice is done.

need-to-breathe.why: Roland blows the oliphant so hard that the veins of his temples burst and blood runs from his mouth, but the strain is in effort more than in air.

hungry.why: No one hungers; the campaign's provisioning is never mentioned.

thirsty.why: No character lacks water, even among the dying at Roncevaux.

sleepy.why: Charlemagne sleeps in his armor and receives Gabriel's dreams of coming battles, and the Franks drop exhausted beside their horses after the pursuit.

nauseous.why: No one sickens from food or poison.

dizzy.why: Roland swoons from his burst temples, the blood-blinded Oliver strikes him in confusion, and Charlemagne faints over Roland's body.

fatigued.why: Roland, spent, strikes Durendal ten times against the rock and cannot break it, and the Franks sleep in their armor after chasing the Saracens to the Ebro.

pain.why: Marsile loses his right hand, Oliver's head is split and his brains run out, and Roland's temples burst from the horn; wounds fill the battle laisses.

disgusted.why: The pagans are painted as monstrous, with the men of Micenes bristled like boars, but revulsion barely figures beside hatred.

over-stimulated.why: The oliphant's blast carries thirty leagues to Charlemagne's ear, but no character is overwhelmed by a sensation.

too-hot-too-cold.why: Storms, hail, and darkness sweep France as portents of Roland's death, but heat and cold never trouble a character.

afraid.why: Ganelon expects death on the embassy and his men weep for him, the Saracens flee Charlemagne into the Ebro, and the pagan army breaks before the Franks.

anxious.why: Charlemagne dreads what Ganelon's choice means for the rearguard, weeps as he rides toward France, and is tormented by dreams of a boar and a leopard.

panic.why: The Saracens, chased by Charlemagne, throw themselves into the Ebro and drown in their armor, and Marsile flees to Saragossa with his hand cut off.

sensory-pleasures.why: Marsile sits on a marble throne in an orchard and Charlemagne holds court in a garden at Cordres, but the senses are given little.

aesthetic-pleasures.why: Durendal's hilt holds relics and the pagans' arms blaze with jewels, but beauty is a sign of worth rather than something anyone enjoys.

fun-excitement.why: The old men play chess and the young ones fence in Charlemagne's orchard before the council, and that is all the play the poem allows.

love-romantic.why: Aude drops dead at Charlemagne's feet when told Roland will not return, and Queen Bramimonde grieves for the maimed Marsile.

love-family.why: Charlemagne mourns his nephew Roland as a son, Baligant weeps for Malprimes, and Ganelon's thirty kinsmen stand surety for him and are hanged.

grief.why: Roland weeps over each dead peer and over Oliver, Charlemagne faints and tears his white beard at Roland's body, and the poem ends in his tears.

missing-someone.why: Charlemagne laments that he has lost his right arm with Roland, and Aude cannot live without him.

liking-as-a-friend.why: Roland and Oliver are sworn companions whose quarrel over the horn and reconciliation at Oliver's death form the poem's heart, and the twelve peers die together.

empathy.why: Roland grieves over each fallen peer in turn, and Charlemagne's barons weep for the dead at Roncevaux.

compassion.why: Archbishop Turpin blesses the dying, Roland carries the bodies of the peers to be absolved, and Charlemagne has the dead gathered and buried.

grateful.why: Charlemagne thanks God when the sun stands still for his pursuit, and Marsile rewards Ganelon with gifts, but gratitude stays in the background.

pleasure-from-helping.why: Turpin serves the dying with absolution, and Thierry steps forward to fight for Charlemagne's cause, but helping is duty, not pleasure.

trustful-distrustful.why: Marsile's false offer of peace, Ganelon's treachery sworn on relics, and Charlemagne's misplaced trust in the embassy set the whole tragedy in motion.

depressed.why: Charlemagne at the end, summoned to yet another war, weeps and calls his life a burden, with his right arm Roland gone.

angry.why: Ganelon's fury when Roland names him envoy, Roland's anger at Marsile's treachery, and Charlemagne's wrath at the Saracens and at Ganelon run through the poem.

envious.why: Ganelon's hatred of Roland is fed by envy of the stepson who is Charlemagne's favorite and the army's pride.

jealous-romantic-sexual.why: No romantic rival threatens any bond; Aude and Roland are betrothed without competition.

jealous-friendship.why: Ganelon resents Roland's place beside Charlemagne, which he reads as a threat to his own standing with the emperor.

hatred.why: Ganelon's hatred of his stepson Roland drives him to betray the rearguard, and Christians and pagans hate each other to the death: pagans are wrong, Christians are right.

contempt.why: Roland scorns Marsile's offer and mocks Ganelon's mission, Oliver tells Roland his recklessness is folly not valor, and all the Franks hold the pagans in contempt.

resentment.why: Ganelon claims he took lawful vengeance for Roland's wrong, not treason, recruits Marsile and then thirty kinsmen to his side, and the trial at Aix turns on that claim.

proud.why: Roland refuses to sound the horn lest his kin be shamed and France lose its renown, and the honor of Charlemagne and the glory of sweet France are invoked on every page.

amused.why: Roland laughs when Ganelon is named envoy, the laugh that Ganelon never forgives; otherwise the poem is grim.

sense-of-belonging.why: Christian Franks against pagan Saracens, the twelve peers, and the cry of sweet France bind every character to a side, and Ganelon's betrayal is a crime against that bond.

lonely.why: Roland dies alone on the field after every companion has fallen, and Charlemagne ends the poem alone with his burden.

judgy-moral-sense.why: The barons first excuse Ganelon, Thierry insists his act was treason against Charlemagne, God decides by combat, and Ganelon is torn apart by four horses.

admiration.why: Pagans and Franks alike marvel at Charlemagne's majesty and Roland's prowess, and Baligant's envoys are struck by the emperor's bearing.

embarrassed.why: Ganelon lets the glove of office fall from his hand before the whole court, an omen that shames him.

shame.why: Roland would rather die than have a shameful song sung of him, Oliver warns that his pride will bring shame on France, and Charlemagne must avenge Roland or be dishonored.

guilt.why: Roland, seeing the peers dead, admits Oliver was right, and Charlemagne reproaches himself for leaving his nephew in the rearguard.

sad.why: Sorrow for the dead at Roncevaux, Aude's death, and Charlemagne's weariness make the poem's second half an extended lament.

happy.why: The Franks rejoice briefly at Charlemagne's return and the fall of Saragossa, but no one's state is good for long.

joyful-euphoric.why: Marsile's court exults when Ganelon delivers Roland to them, and the Franks rejoice when Saragossa falls and Baligant dies.

effort.why: Roland pushes his dying body to blow the horn, break Durendal, and carry the peers to Turpin, and Charlemagne's seven years of war end only to begin anew.

focused-in-flow.why: The peers in combat strike blow after blow in a trance of slaughter described laisse by laisse, each blow cleaving a Saracen to the saddle.

bored.why: Nothing in the poem is idle long enough to bore anyone.

distracted.why: No character's attention wanders from the matter at hand.

impatient.why: Roland is eager for battle and refuses delay, but impatience barely registers.

curious.why: No character investigates or wonders; the Franks ask only who will go as envoy and who will hold the rearguard.

surprised.why: Oliver climbs a hill and is stunned to see the pagan host, Charlemagne hears the horn and knows the truth, and Aude's sudden death astonishes the court.

awe.why: The sun stands still at Charlemagne's prayer, storms and darkness cover France as Roland dies, and angels carry his soul to paradise.

skeptical-doubtful.why: Roland doubts Marsile's offer and cites his past treachery, Oliver doubts the wisdom of refusing the horn, and Charlemagne doubts Ganelon's claim that the horn means a hunt.

feeling-of-knowing.why: No character strains after a half-remembered fact.

confused.why: Oliver, blinded by blood, strikes Roland by mistake and asks who it is, and Charlemagne's barons are at a loss over Ganelon's plea.

frustrated.why: Roland strikes Durendal against the rock and cannot break it, and Charlemagne, who thought the war won, is called by Gabriel to fight again.

uncertain-certain.why: Charlemagne's council weighs Marsile's offer, Roland and Oliver argue three times over the horn, and the barons waver over Ganelon's guilt until the duel decides.

understanding.why: At the horn's sound Charlemagne understands at once that Ganelon has betrayed the rearguard, and Roland sees the truth of Oliver's counsel too late.

inspired.why: Ganelon devises the ambush with Marsile and Thierry finds the argument that condemns him, but insight is not the poem's register.

satisfied.why: Justice is done on Ganelon and Saragossa is won, yet Charlemagne finds no rest, for God calls him to a new war as the poem closes.

foreboding.why: Charlemagne's dreams of a boar and a leopard, Ganelon's dropped glove, and the storms over France all foretell the disaster at Roncevaux.

nostalgia.why: Dying, Roland recalls the lands he conquered, sweet France, his lineage, and Charlemagne who raised him.

anticipation-suspense.why: The Franks ride into the pass knowing the pagans are massed, Charlemagne hears the horn and races back too late, and the duel of Pinabel and Thierry hangs in the balance.

hope.why: Roland blows the horn hoping Charlemagne will return to avenge them, and the dying Franks hope for paradise, which Turpin promises.

schadenfreude.why: Ganelon relishes Roland's coming death as he plots with Marsile, and the pagans gloat that they will have the Franks' heads.

elevation.why: Roland's death, facing Spain and holding up his glove to God, and Thierry's lone stand for justice against Pinabel lift the poem's moral register.

rage.why: Roland rides through the pagans in a fury after Oliver's death, and Charlemagne pursues the Saracens to the Ebro in a vengeful rage.
